ChiShona is taught using this same national structure as isiNdebele, in the learner's own language. chunks.topic: Structure of the Indigenous Languages Syllabus
chunks.content: ChiShona is taught under the national Indigenous Languages syllabus, which covers ECD A through Grade 7 as a single spiral curriculum: the same four skills (Listening/Observing, Speaking/Signing, Reading, Writing/Brailling) and broadly the same topics are covered at every grade, gaining in breadth and depth as learners progress. At the Infant level (ECD A - Grade 2), the learner's indigenous language (ChiShona in Shona-speaking areas) serves as the medium of instruction across the whole curriculum, not just as a language subject. From Grade 3, it continues as a dedicated subject alongside English. The syllabus is explicitly designed to inculcate the values of Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu and to promote and cherish Zimbabwean identity.

At Junior level, ChiShona is assessed through continuous assessment (30% of the final mark, covering drawing, speaking, written exercises, theory exercises, and research projects on culture and heritage) and summative assessment (70%). Summative assessment has two papers: Paper 1 (40 marks) consists of 40 multiple-choice questions covering register, aspects of culture, comprehension, language usage and language structure; Paper 2 (30 marks) has Section A (composition - candidates choose one from five questions) and Section B (comprehension and summary, 5 marks each).

Listening/Observing topics progress from Grade 3's sounds made by objects/animals/materials, word sounds, rhymes/jingles/riddles, dialogue, news/stories/folktales, instructions and times of day; through Grade 4-5's phonetic sounds, totems, sustained dialogue and stress/intonation work; to Grade 6-7's debates on cross-cutting themes, voice and mood in speech, and messages from different media. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to retell folktales, identify moral lessons from folktales, and demonstrate understanding by answering questions. Common activities include storytelling, retelling stories and news, drama, role play, memory games, and singing songs and rhymes to strengthen listening skills.
learning_activities: Listening to and retelling ChiShona folktales, identifying the moral lesson (dzidziso)
Playing sound and memory games with radios, percussion instruments and ICT tools
Listening to and discussing debates on cross-cutting themes in upper grades

chunks.content: Speaking/Signing topics progress from Grade 3's likes/dislikes, roles of self and family members, counting games, reciting rhymes and folktales; through Grade 4-6's totems, myths and taboos, heritage sites, natural resources, debates on cross-cutting themes, and appropriate registers/requests; to Grade 7's prepared and unprepared speeches, riddles/idioms/proverbs, common myths and legends, and figurative expressions. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to tell stories on emerging and cross-cutting themes, debate, dramatise, recite poems and rhymes, and retell folktales.
learning_activities: Reciting rhymes, jingles and riddles (zvirahwe) in ChiShona
Debating cross-cutting themes using appropriate register
Presenting prepared and unprepared speeches by Grade 7

chunks.content: Reading topics progress from Grade 3's syllable sounds, words and sentences, news/stories/folktales, extensive reading, and simple graphs/maps/tables; through Grade 4-6's meanings of words from context, referencing skills, skimming and scanning, idioms/similes/proverbs/ideophones (zvirungamutauro), and inferences; to Grade 7's modern and ancient ways of communication, and continued work on comprehension, intonation and enunciation. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to read a variety of materials, demonstrate understanding through answering questions, and comment on emerging and cross-cutting issues read.
learning_activities: Reading ChiShona texts for comprehension and identifying idioms and proverbs (tsumo)
Practising skimming and scanning skills on graphs, maps and tables in Shona
Discussing modern and traditional ways of communication in Grade 7

chunks.content: Writing/Brailling topics progress from Grade 3's Nelson's script handwriting, punctuation, comprehension questions, creative writing, spelling and dictation, composition, and idioms/riddles/similes/proverbs; through Grade 4-6's poems and prose, summaries, business and friendly letters, telegrams, emails, blogs, essays with linking paragraphs, and information from graphs/pictures/tables; to Grade 7's continued essays, short stories, folktales, creative work, comprehension, summary, spelling, dictation and punctuation, plus ICT tools in writing throughout. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to write creative works, write in appropriate register, and write with grammatical accuracy, correct spelling and appropriate punctuation.
learning_activities: Practising Nelson's script handwriting in ChiShona from Grade 3
Writing formal and informal letters in ChiShona by Grade 5-6
Composing essays, short stories and folktales with correct spelling and punctuation by Grade 7

chunks.content: Common ChiShona greetings: 'Mhoro' (Hello, informal, singular), 'Mhoroi' (Hello, formal/plural or to an elder), 'Makadii?' (How are you? - formal/plural), 'Wakadii?' (How are you? - informal, singular), 'Ndiripo, makadiiwo?' (I am fine, and how are you?), 'Ndiri kunzwa zvakanaka' (I am feeling well). Time-of-day greetings: 'Mangwanani' (Good morning), 'Masikati' (Good afternoon), 'Manheru' (Good evening). Farewells: 'Chisarai zvakanaka' (Stay well, said by the one leaving) / 'Fambai zvakanaka' (Go well, said by the one staying). 'Ndatenda' or 'Maita basa' means thank you; 'Ndine urombo' means I am sorry.

ChiShona numbers 1-10: potsi/imwe chete (1), piri (2), tatu (3), china (4), shanu (5), tanhatu (6), nomwe (7), sere (8), pfumbamwe (9), gumi (10). Numbers 11-20 are typically formed as 'gumi ne-X' (ten and X): gumi neimwe (11), gumi nembiri (12), gumi netatu (13), continuing to makumi maviri (20, literally 'two tens'). Note that ChiShona numbers agree grammatically with the noun class of the object being counted (concordial agreement), so the exact form of the number word changes depending on what is being counted - e.g. 'vana vaviri' (two children) versus 'mabhuku maviri' (two books).

Common ChiShona family/kinship terms: 'Amai' (mother), 'Baba' (father), 'Mwana' (child), 'Mukoma' (older brother, used by a younger sibling), 'Munin'ina' (younger sibling of the same sex), 'Hanzvadzi' (sibling of the opposite sex), 'Sekuru' (grandfather / maternal uncle - an important culturally significant relative), 'Ambuya' or 'Mbuya' (grandmother), 'Tete' (paternal aunt - also an important culturally significant relative in Shona custom), 'Sahwira' (a close family friend with special ceremonial roles). Shona kinship terms often carry specific cultural roles and responsibilities beyond the direct English translation - for example, 'Sekuru' and 'Tete' have recognised roles in family ceremonies and guidance.

chunks.topic: Days of the Week and Time (Mazuva)
chunks.content: ChiShona days of the week: Muvhuro (Monday), Chipiri (Tuesday), Chitatu (Wednesday), China (Thursday), Chishanu (Friday), Mugovera (Saturday), Svondo (Sunday). Time-related vocabulary: 'Nhasi' (today), 'Mangwana' (tomorrow), 'Nezuro' (yesterday), 'Gore' (year), 'Mwedzi' (month), 'Vhiki' (week, a loanword).

ChiShona, like other Bantu languages, organises nouns into noun classes, each marked by a characteristic prefix, which also determines the agreement pattern for adjectives, verbs and pronouns referring to that noun. Common classes include: Class 1/2 (mu-/va-, mostly people, e.g. 'munhu' person / 'vanhu' people), Class 3/4 (mu-/mi-, mostly plants and objects, e.g. 'muti' tree / 'miti' trees), Class 5/6 (ri-(or zero)/ma-, e.g. 'zino' tooth / 'meno' teeth), Class 7/8 (chi-/zvi-, e.g. 'chinhu' thing / 'zvinhu' things), and Class 9/10 (N-/N-, often animals, e.g. 'imbwa' dog / 'imbwa' dogs, same form but different agreement). Understanding noun class is essential because it drives subject-verb agreement and adjective agreement throughout a ChiShona sentence.

Common ChiShona colour terms: 'Chena' (white), 'Tema' (black), 'Tsvuku' (red), 'Girini' (green, a loanword; also described descriptively), 'Bhuruu' (blue, a loanword). Basic descriptive adjectives: 'Kukura' (big), 'Kudiki'/'kudoko' (small), 'Refu' (long/tall), 'Pfupi' (short), 'Chakanaka' (good/nice), 'Chakaipa' (bad). As with nouns, adjectives take a prefix that agrees with the noun class of the thing being described.

Useful everyday ChiShona phrases: 'Ndinoda mvura' (I want water), 'Ndine nzara' (I am hungry, literally 'I have hunger'), 'Ndiri kuenda kuchikoro' (I am going to school), 'Munonzi ani?' (What is your name? - formal), 'Ndinonzi...' (My name is...), 'Ndapota' (Please), 'Hongu' (Yes), 'Kwete' (No), 'Ndiripo' (I am here/fine), 'Handisi kunzwa' (I don't understand / I can't hear).

Totems (mitupo) are a distinctive feature of Shona culture, functioning as clan identifiers passed down patrilineally, usually associated with an animal or natural object (e.g. Shumba/lion, Moyo/heart, Nzou/elephant, Shava/eland, Soko/monkey). Each totem is typically accompanied by praise names (zvidawo) recited to show respect, especially to elders, and totems play an important role in regulating marriage customs (people sharing the same totem are traditionally considered too closely related to marry) and in identity and respect within Shona society. The syllabus's Speaking/Listening strands reference totems from Grade 4 onward, building in depth through to Grade 7's inclusion of totems and their poems (nhetembo dzemitupo).
